Learning Objectives
Discuss the basic principles of and risks associated with irradiation for patients and operators
of imaging equipment.
Identify methods to reduce the risks associated with irradiation to patients and operators of
imaging equipment.
Determine the most appropriate methods for counseling for patients on the risk associated
with irradiation.
Overview

radiation to form an image. Other imaging modalities (ultrasonography, MRI) do not involve

the use of ionizing radiation to form an image.
Ionizing radiation has biologic effects on cells that may range from repairable damage to

Effects of ionizing radiation are classified into deterministic and stochastic effects.
Deterministic effects, such as cataracts, are dose-dependent and occur after exposure to

Introduction
Exposure to ionizing radiation mostly results from natural background radiation and exposure
during medical procedures involving imaging.
Ionizing radiation can cause biologic effects in living cells that may become precursors to
malignancy.

Introduction
Ionizing radiation can cause biologic effects in living cells ranging from unimportant,
repairable cell damage to extreme cases of cellular damage that may lead to cancer.1,2
The two main sources of irradiation are background radiation and radiation used for
medical procedures (Resource 1). Background radiation emanates from radioactive
materials naturally present in the air and soil and from space in the form of cosmic
radiation. The mean background radiation exposure in the United States is
approximately 3.1 mSv per year; however, this value varies based on geographic
location. Living at higher altitudes increases exposure to cosmic radiation; cosmic
radiation exposure for individuals living in Colorado Springs, Colorado, is approximately
0.8 mSv. Living at sea level is associated with decreased exposure to cosmic radiation,
approximately 0.3 mSv.
The mean annual radiation exposure from medical procedures varies by country. In the
United States, the contribution from medical procedures to the overall mean effective
dose steeply increased from 15% in the early 1980s to 48% in 2006. CT and nuclear

medicine were responsible for most medical exposure. However, medical exposures in
the United States have decreased since 2006 because of several factors, including
increased awareness of radiation safety (Resource 2).
Physics of Radiation
Radiation can be ionizing or nonionizing.
Ionizing radiation is used for radiography, CT, and nuclear medicine.
Ionizing radiation deposits energy into tissues. The effect of this energy depends on the
absorbed dose, or energy per kilogram of tissue, and the effective dose.
The effective dose involves consideration that some tissues (such as the breasts or lungs) are
more sensitive to the effects of radiation than other tissues (such as bone).

Physics of Radiation
Radiation is a form of energy that can be classified as ionizing or nonionizing radiation,
depending on its energy level.3 Ionizing radiation, such as that used for radiography and
nuclear medicine, is associated with higher energy levels. Radio waves used for MRI and
sound waves used for ultrasonography are nonionizing.3
Ionizing radiation deposits energy in tissue via excitation and ionization. To determine
the potential effects of this radiation, the amount of energy absorbed (absorbed dose)
and the sensitivity of those tissues to the effects of radiation (effective dose) must be
considered.4 Absorbed dose in tissue is defined as the energy imparted by ionizing
radiation per unit mass of the irradiated tissue. The International System unit for
absorbed dose is Gray (Gy), in which 1 Gy = 1 joule/kg. The older unit for absorbed dose
is the rad (1 Gy = 100 rad).
The different energies of ionizing radiation are not considered in the absorbed. Another
unit, equivalent dose (H), considers that some radiation, such as alpha particles, will have
a higher amount of energy deposited per unit of absorbed dose.4 The International

System unit for equivalent dose is the Sievert, in which 1 Sievert (Sv) = 1 joule/kg. The
older unit for equivalent dose is the rem (1 Sv = 100 rem).
Effective dose (E) is a calculated value that considers the varying biologic sensitivity of
different tissues (eg, lung and breast tissues are more sensitive to ionizing radiation than
brain tissue). For medical imaging procedures, typically only a portion of the body is
exposed; therefore, only those organs receiving a dose contribute to the calculated
estimate of the effective dose. The effective doses of various imaging modalities are
listed in Table 1.
The effective dose is used widely in the literature as a metric for specific radiologic
procedures; however, the risk to a specific person is not considered in the effective dose,
nor is sex, age, and other patient-specific factors.5

Biology and Radiation
Ionizing radiation can alter the DNA of living cells.
The effects of ionizing radiation are classified into deterministic and stochastic effects.
Deterministic effects, such as cataracts, are dose-dependent and occur after exposure to
radiation doses higher than specific thresholds.
Stochastic effects, such as cancer, may result from exposure to any dose without a specific
threshold.

Biology and Radiation
Ionizing radiation can alter physiologic processes, leading to cell death and causing
changes in DNA.2 DNA changes often are detected and corrected by cell repair
mechanisms; however, some DNA defects may persist. Different human cells have
different sensitivity to ionizing radiation; for example, muscle cells and chondrocytes are
less sensitive to irradiation than lymphocytes, endothelium, or other rapidly dividing
cells. These characteristics of radiation can be used in a targeted manner to manage
certain malignant tumors.
The biologic effects of ionizing radiation are classified as deterministic or stochastic.2
Deterministic effects are dose-dependent and occur after exposure to radiation doses
higher than specific thresholds. Stochastic effects may result from exposure to any dose

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004012
5/19

of radiation without a specific threshold. Examples of deterministic effects include skin
erythema, cataracts, and fetal malformation.
A stochastic effect is cancer induction.2 At lower radiation doses, the risk of cancer
induction is difficult to determine because of the relatively high incidence of cancer in
the general population; however, most institutions in the United States operate
according to the as-low-as-reasonably-achievable (ALARA) principle. According to ALARA,
any increase in dose results in an incremental increase in radiation risk.
Imaging Modalities
Imaging modalities that involve the use ionizing radiation include fluoroscopy, radiography, CT,
and nuclear medicine.
Fluoroscopy units should track the radiation dose to the patient per The Joint Commission
standards.
An accumulative dose higher than 15 Gy to a single field within a period of 6 months is
considered a reviewable sentinel event by The Joint Commission.

Imaging Modalities
Fluoroscopy is routinely used during orthopaedic surgical procedures. Fluoroscopy units
can be fixed or portable.6 Fixed units can be under the table or overhead, depending on
the x-ray tube position (under or over the table). Portable fluoroscopy units, in which the
x-ray tube and the image receptor in the form of a “C” can be rotated around 360°
angles, commonly are used in orthopaedics (Figure 1). Portable fluoroscopy units can be
regular sized C-arms or mini C-arms.
The components of a typical fluoroscopy C-arm are an x-ray tube, image receptor (image
intensifier or flat panel), collimator, display monitor, and x-ray generator/controls. Per
The Joint Commission standards, patient fluoroscopy doses should be tracked.
Prolonged fluoroscopy with a cumulative dose higher than 15 Gy to a single field within a
period of 6 months is defined as a reviewable sentinel event by The Joint Commission.7

Mini C-arms (Figure 2) are increasingly used in orthopaedics because of their compact
size and portability. The exposure rate from a mini C-arm is substantially lower that than
of a standard C-arm; however, because of their compact size, the operator of a mini C-
arm needs to be closer to the x-ray tube. This may increase operator exposure to scatter
dose. With these compact fluoroscopy units, particular attention is necessary to protect
the operator’s hands from x-ray beam exposure.8

Reducing Irradiation Risk
Patients
Techniques that decrease radiation dose during fluoroscopy and should be used as often as
possible include the following:
Minimize time
Last image hold (a setting in which the monitor keeps the last image that was obtained)
Maximize the distance between the patient and the x-ray tube
Minimize the distance between the patient and the image receptor
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM
AAOS | Radiation Safety
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004012
8/19

Use pulsed fluoroscopy or a lower frame rate
Collimate
Techniques that increase radiation dose during fluoroscopy and should be avoided as often as
possible include the following:
Digital acquisition
Cine runs
Magnification modes
High dose or boost modes

Patients
The ALARA principle should be followed to minimize patient and operator radiation dose
exposures.9 To adhere to the ALARA principle, equipment operators must an
understanding of fluoroscopy equipment capabilities and underlying radiation safety
principles. The age-old wisdom of time, distance and shielding always is a good starting
point.
10 Fluoroscopy time should be minimized, and last image hold should be used if
available. Because patient dose has an inverse square dependence with distance from
the x-ray tube, the patient–x-ray tube distance should be maximized to decrease the
patient skin entrance dose. Doubling the distance decreases the radiation dose to one-
quarter of the original dose. Spacer cones should always be attached to the x-ray tube to
ensure that a minimum distance of 20 cm is maintained between the patient and the x-
ray tube. In automatic exposure rate control driven C-arms, the distance from the
patient to the image receptor should be minimized to attain a lower technique (kV and
mA).10 Pulsed fluoroscopy and lower frame rate should be used if feasible. For example,
15 frames per second (fps) typically has one-half the dose rate of 30 fps; even lower
rates, such as 7.5 fps and 3.75 fps, can be used in situations that do not require high
temporal resolution. Frequent C-arm rotation and appropriate use of collimation
(reducing the field of view to include only the area of interest) are recommended to
further reduce patient dose.
Collimation of the x-ray beam to the area of interest reduces irradiation dose and
increases image quality.11 Digital acquisition or cine runs typically are associated with
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004012
9/19

dose rates 10 to 60 times higher than normal fluoroscopy mode and should be used
sparingly.
Magnification modes result in a higher patient dose and should only be used if
appropriate. Normal fluoroscopy and, preferably, low-dose modes should be used on a
routine basis. High-dose or boost modes rarely should be used.11
In CT, the amount of radiation is dependent on the length of the body part scanned;
therefore, if possible (eg, in follow-up imaging of pars fractures), the imaging study
should be limited to the area of interest.
Operators of Imaging Equipment
Operators should be aware of the potential effects of radiation exposure and methods to
reduce exposure.
The x-ray tube should be facing up through the table, with the image intensifier above the
patient. For a lateral view, the operator should stand on the image receptor side of the table.
Techniques to reduce the dose to the patient also will reduce the dose to the operator.
Other techniques to reduce the dose to the operator include the following:
Shielding (lead aprons, thyroid shield, leaded glasses, leaded gloves, table drapes)
Keep hands out of the field
Consider operator position and distance relative to the patient. Increasing distance
exponentially decreases the radiation dose (Table 2).


Operators of Imaging Equipment
The patient is not the only individual exposed to radiation during medical procedures.
The operator and all other individuals in the room at the time of imaging also are
exposed to radiation. Operators who perform multiple and/or lengthy procedures that
involve the use ionizing radiation should be aware of the potential effects they are
exposed to and methods to reduce their exposure.
Dose-saving techniques to the patient also lead to a lower scatter dose to the operator.
Shielding in the form of lead aprons, thyroid shield, leaded gloves, and leaded glasses
should be used by the operator during a fluoroscopy procedure, and all others who are
exposed should be shielded.12 Protective devices may give a false sense of security and
often are only partially protective. Most gloves (except for thick, heavy, clumsy ones) are
meant to protect from indirect irradiation but not the direct x-ray beam. Typical lead
thickness of 0.25 mm to 0.5 mm will block more than 90% of the scattered x-rays.
Ceiling-mounted lead screens and under-table lead drapes should be used if available.

To ensure appropriate protection, lead aprons must be inspected annually. An
inspection tag should be placed on the apron, and the date of the inspection should be
stored in a database. Aprons should be stored on hangers immediately after use.
Improperly stored lead aprons may become cracked or damaged, reducing their
effectiveness.13
Hands should always be kept outside the x-ray beam to minimize operator extremity
dose. With AP C-arm positioning, the scatter dose is higher under the table; therefore,
table drapes (if available) should be used to minimize exposure to the legs (Figure 3).
With lateral C-arm positioning, the scatter dose is much higher on the x-ray tube side;
therefore, if possible, the operator should stand on the image receptor side. With an
increase in distance from the scattering source, scatter radiation decreases rapidly;
therefore, operators should maximize distance from the patient as much as possible.12
Medical professionals who perform examinations that involve the use of ionizing
radiation should wear a dosimetry badge to assess their individual exposure. The badge
should be worn outside of the lead shield protection. The location that best estimates
the dose to the thyroid and eyes is at the neck, at which most dosimetry badges should
be placed. Federal guidelines are available on the amount of dose that an operator
should receive per year, including whole body and eye doses, and specific doses for
pregnant workers.
To mitigate the risk of irradiation, each institution should have a dedicated quality
control program to optimize image quality and assess exposure risk. Such quality control
programs should be supervised by a medical physicist.

Counseling on Irradiation Risk
Accurately presenting the potential risk of irradiation to patients is difficult.
For many procedures, the irradiation dose is so low that the risk is not defined.
The ALARA principle should always be followed.

Counseling on Irradiation Risk
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:56 PM
AAOS | Radiation Safety
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004012
13/19

Informed consent is not required for most procedures that result in ionizing radiation
(eg, routine radiography or CT); however, patients are increasingly aware of the potential
effects of irradiation and may ask questions about their risk. In some situations, such as
fluoroscopy procedures or in sensitive patient populations (eg, pregnant or pediatric
patients), informed consent may be considered. Unfortunately, layman understanding of
irradiation risk is limited, and the risk must be weighed against the advantages. The risk
of irradiation dose generally is quite low from diagnostic imaging. Dose calculators can
provide the increased cancer risk and the relative irradiation and risk compared with
other activities (eg, flying, driving, living in New York City). For example, a PA chest
radiograph is the equivalent of 2.4 days of mean background irradiation or
approximately one cross-continental flight. A pelvic radiograph is equivalent to 3 months
of mean background irradiation, and an abdominal CT scan is equivalent to 2.5 years of
mean background irradiation (Table 3; Resource 3).
Until recently, gonadal and fetal shielding was standard in radiology departments. That
policy has been re-examined and deemed to be inappropriate. As recently stated in a
white paper by the American Association of Physicists in Medicine, shielding
paradoxically increases the dose to those structures that are meant to be protected.14,15
(Resource 4); however, shielding is still required by law in some states and hospitals but
is a practice that should eventually be discontinued.
